name: Boric acid (put in the vagina; poisonous if swallowed)
short: Swallowed boric acid has killed infants (5 of 11 newborns fed it by mistake died); skin contact has been fatal. Vaginal: burning under 10%, mostly mild; sparse data; guidelines: avoid in pregnancy.
text: This entry covers boric acid put in the vagina (capsules, inserts or gel); the poisoning data below come from boric acid swallowed or put on the skin, not from vaginal use. Swallowed: a 2021 toxicity review states that fatalities have occurred after oral ingestion and that skin exposure has proven fatal in some cases. A case report describes an 18-month-old child who died after accidentally eating a boric acid roach pesticide, and its authors say most documented borate deaths have been in infants; they also say borates were once used to irrigate body cavities, including the vagina, until their toxicity and potential lethality were recognised. In a 1964 report from a newborn nursery, 11 infants were poisoned when boric acid was used by mistake in preparing their formula feeds, and 5 of them died; a 2015 record with no abstract is titled as treatment of boric acid overdose in two infants with continuous haemodialysis, without naming the route. A 1949 record is titled as a report of six accidental deaths in infants, and a 2022 record is titled as a case of boric acid poisoning with life-threatening corrosive injury and liver, kidney and lung failure, without naming the route (neither has an abstract). Seven infants had seizures from repeated ingestion after a soother was dipped in a borax and honey mixture, and a 1987 review calls misuse of boric acid antiseptics one of the most common causes of poisoning accidents in newborns and infants. On the other side, in a poison-centre series of 784 ingestions, all but 2 of them single (acute) ingestions, no one developed severe toxicity and 88.3% had no symptoms; in another series of 364 exposures there was one death, from probable repeated ingestion, and vomiting, nausea, diarrhoea and cramps were common. In the vagina: a review of 14 studies (2 randomised trials, 9 case series and 4 case reports, in vaginal yeast infection) found vaginal burning in under 10% of cases, watery discharge and vaginal redness. In women with recurrent bacterial vaginosis, no adverse effects were observed in a 58-woman chart review, and mild adverse events occurred in 7.8% of a 52-woman observational study; in a randomised trial of a boric acid-based vaginal gel or insert in 106 women with bacterial vaginosis, vaginal yeast infection or both, vulvovaginal burning was the most common adverse event (9.6%). A chart review of maintenance use (average 13 months) reports few adverse events, without figures. A 2021 narrative review says safety data are sparse and that available data suggest vaginal use is safe at doses commonly prescribed, but that information on harms in pregnancy is limited and guidelines recommend avoiding it in pregnancy; the 2021 toxicity review reports reproductive toxicity as an endpoint in animals and reduced foetal weight in one animal inhalation study (animal data only); a 2006 record titled as a study of teratogenic effects of vaginal boric acid in pregnancy has no abstract, so its findings cannot be reported. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
